study.title: Micah 1 The LORD comes in judgment against Samaria and Jerusalem
study.overview: The chapter opens with the presentation of the prophet and with a solemn call for everyone to hear. The message is of divine judgment against the idolatry and the corruption of Samaria and Jerusalem, showing that the sin of Israel and Judah is not overlooked before the God who reigns from his holy temple. The judgment is described with images of earthquake, collapse of walls and public lament, culminating in a final statement of deep mourning, as if the mother city lost its children in captivity.

outline.title: Presentation of the word and call to listen
outline.explanation: The book is presented as the word of the LORD received by Micah in the days of three kings of Judah. Then all the earth is called to pay attention, because God himself rises up as a witness against his people since his holy temple.

outline.title: The Lord comes to judge the idolatry of Samaria
outline.explanation: The language describes the LORD coming out of his place to tread the highs of the earth. Mountains and valleys undo before him, for judgment comes because of Jacob's transgression. Samaria is announced as a ruin, her images will be broken and her wealth linked to the cultual prostitution will be destroyed.

outline.title: The prophet laments and the scope of judgment widens
outline.explanation: Micah answers the announcement with tear, barefoot and naked, as a sign of public pain. The wounds of sin have already reached Judah and came to Jerusalem. The cities mentioned in sequence show the shame, the mourning and the approach of evil to the door of Jerusalem.

outline.title: The cities of Judah and the mourning of captivity
outline.explanation: Laquis is warned, for his transgressions have spread; other localities are associated with deception, defeat and humiliation. The chapter ends with order to shave the head in mourning by the children taken in captivity, as a sign of deep loss and exile.

study.context: According to the notes, Micah was of Moresheth, and prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. These reigns cover approximately a long period, and the message of the chapter relates to the context of the threat and fall of Samaria, in addition to the advance of judgment also on Judah. The notes also note that "Samaria" and "Jerusalem" can function both as cities and as representatives of their respective kingdoms.
study.theology: The chapter presents God as King and Holy Judge, who does not tolerate the covenant with idolatry or false religious security. His judgment is not arbitrary: he responds to the transgression of the covenant, to the corruption of the leaders, and to the unfaithfulness of the people. The image of the LORD coming out of his place emphasizes his sovereignty and his historical action against sin. There is also a strong pastoral aspect: the prophet does not announce the sentence as an indifferent person, but as one who weeps with the people, showing that the true proclamation of divine judgment includes pain, urgency and implicit call to repentance. The chapter further teaches that the sin of a people can spread and reach neighboring regions, and that idolatry corrupts even what seems wealth or security.

scholarViews.insight: The expressions "Samaria" and "Jerusalem" can appoint not only the cities, but also their entire kingdoms; judgment begins against Samaria and shows that God is coming to judge his people.
Prophecy is presented as the word of the LORD, that is, divine revelation that must be received with reverence, not as human opinion.
The order to shave the head expresses great grief and despair, and the chapter ends up pointing to captivity as a fulfillment of the announced desolation.

questions: What changes in my way of listening to the Bible when I receive it as a word of the LORD and not just as religious information?
What forms of idolatry or false trust can be corrupting the lives of God's people today, as Samaria and Jerusalem have corrupted?
My reaction to God's sin and judgment seems more like indifference or with the mourning and seriousness of Micah?
study.practice: Read the chapter as a call to personal and community repentance. Examine whether there are areas in which you are relying on structures, religious appearance or mixed commitments to sin. Pray that God will give you sensitivity to mourn evil without hardening your heart, and practice a faith that responds to the Lord with humility, confession and concrete obedience.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the general identification of Micah, the period of the cited kings and the broad sense of judgment; however, some historical details and the exact correspondence of certain names of cities with specific locations remain uncertain or depend on traditional identification. It is also not possible to confirm by the material given all geographical and chronological associations with absolute precision.
